title: The Year of the Elephant
subtitle: Before his birth, the world already bowed to his coming
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1, pp. 43-54 and 158 — Abraha, al-Qulays, the elephant, the birds, and the birth in the Year of the Elephant
Qur'an 105 (Surah Al-Fil) — the companions of the elephant

chapters.heading: Abraha's Army and the Falling Birds
chapters.body: In the year the Prophet ﷺ was born, Abraha al-Ashram, who had taken control of Yemen, built a church in Sana'a (al-Qulays) and wrote to the Negus that he would not stop until he had diverted the Arabs' pilgrimage to it. When Abraha learned that a man of Kinana had gone into the church and done something in it, he swore to march on the House and demolish it, and set out with an elephant (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, pp. 43-45). The Qur'an compressed the end of that march into five verses: 'Have you not considered, [O Muhammad], how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plan into misguidance? And He sent against them birds in flocks, Striking them with stones of hard clay, And He made them like eaten straw' (105:1-5). Ibn Hisham's account has birds coming from the sea, each carrying three stones, the army fleeing and dying along the roads, and Abraha himself dying at Sana'a (vol. 1, pp. 53-54). Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet ﷺ was born on a Monday, the twelfth of Rabi' al-Awwal, in the Year of the Elephant (vol. 1, p. 158; the editor notes other views on the month). The House that had been defended that year is the House that would become the qiblah of the world.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Allah defended His House with birds. What big threat in your life might look smaller if you remembered Who is defending you?

title: The Orphan of Makkah
subtitle: Amina's son, Halimah's milk, Abu Talib's shadow
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1, pp. 158-179 — the birth, the fosterage with Banu Sa'd, Amina's death, Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Talib
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — Halimah's account of the fosterage (vol. 1, pp. 161-165; not from the six books; Not yet scholar-reviewed)

chapters.heading: The Child Who Brought Blessing
chapters.body: Muhammad ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant, son of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Amina bint Wahb. Ibn Ishaq has Abdullah die while Amina was still pregnant (the editor notes the view that he died when the child was a few months old). Abd al-Muttalib looked for wet nurses and a woman of Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr, Halimah bint Abi Dhu'ayb, took him. In her own account, it was a year of drought; her old she-camel gave no milk and her own milk was too little for her son. After she took the orphan, her breasts gave milk, the camel's udder was full, and her donkey outpaced the caravan (seerah report: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, pp. 161-163; not from the six books). When she brought him back, Amina asked why she returned him, since she had been eager to keep him. At six, his mother Amina died at al-Abwa, between Makkah and Madinah, on the way back from visiting his maternal kin in Madinah. He stayed with his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib, for whom a cushion was set in the shade of the Kaaba; his sons sat around it and none sat on it, but the boy would come and sit on it, and when his uncles pulled him away Abd al-Muttalib told them to leave his son alone and sat him beside him. Ibn Ishaq says Abd al-Muttalib died when the Prophet ﷺ was eight (some say ten), and Abu Talib then took charge of his affairs. The Qur'an would one day name his condition over him: 'Did He not find you an orphan and give [you] refuge?' (93:6). Orphanhood was his first teacher; protection was his Lord's first gift.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ lost his parents as a small child and was still raised with love. Who shelters the vulnerable people around you — and could that be you?

title: Al-Amin, The Trustworthy
subtitle: The honest young man the Quraysh could not bribe
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 187-189 and 198 (Maysarah, the marriage, al-Amin), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — Khadijah's testimony to his character

chapters.heading: The Merchant of Makkah
chapters.body: As a young man Muhammad ﷺ was known among Quraysh for the truth of his speech and his great trustworthiness, and Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, a woman of standing who hired men to trade with her wealth, sent him to Syria with her slave Maysarah on better terms than she gave other merchants (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 188). The goods sold for double or close to it. Maysarah told her what he had seen, including, in his report, two angels shading Muhammad ﷺ from the sun; that is Maysarah's report as Ibn Ishaq passes it on, not a hadith. Khadijah then sent to him and said that she wished to marry him because of his kinship, his standing among his people, his trustworthiness, his good character and the truth of his speech (p. 189); a footnote names Nafisa bint Munya as the go-between on another account. She is given as forty and he twenty-five (p. 187; a note says another view makes her forty-five). Years later, when revelation first shook him, her answer named the character of his whole youth: 'You keep good relations with your kin, you help the weak, you honor the guest, you bear the hardship of the road, you help against the calamities of truth' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3). And Ibn Hisham notes that before revelation Quraysh called him al-Amin, the Trustworthy (p. 198).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Khadijah listed five habits that proved his prophethood. Which of the five — kin, the weak, guests, hardship, truth — needs your work this month?

title: The Cave of Hira
subtitle: Forty years of silence before the first word
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the retreat to Hira
Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — Aisha's narration of the first revelation
Qur'an 96:1-5 — the first revealed words

chapters.heading: Solitude Before the Storm
chapters.body: In his late thirties, Muhammad ﷺ began leaving Makkah's noise for the cave of Hira on Jabal an-Nur, taking provisions and turning his face to the silence. The seerah records that he would stay days at a time in the cave, thinking — a man of Makkah withdrawing from Makkah, troubled by the idols he had never bowed to. In the month of Ramadan, in the year he turned forty, the silence ended. The angel came to him and said: Iqra — Read. He answered: I am not one who can read. The angel embraced him until it was more than he could bear, then released him and repeated the command — three times — until the words descended: 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created - Created man from a clinging substance. Recite, and your Lord is the most Generous - Who taught by the pen - Taught man that which he knew not' (96:1-5). The first word of the final revelation was not a command to rule or to fight. It was a command to read, in the name of the One who created — and the first description of the Lord it gave was not power, but generosity (96:3).

chapters.heading: Khadijah's Test
chapters.body: He ran home from the cave trembling, asking to be covered, and told Khadijah what he had seen — and her response, preserved in Bukhari's Sahih, became the first theology of the new religion: 'Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep good relations with your kin, you help the weak, you honor the guest, you bear the hardship of the road, you help against the calamities of truth' (Bukhari 3). Notice: his wife reasoned from character to truth. Then she took him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal, a Christian scholar, who heard the description and said the words that confirmed everything: 'This is the same one who keeps the secrets whom Allah had sent to Moses' (Bukhari 3). The first consultant of the prophethood was a woman; the first confirmation came from a Christian scholar who knew the scriptures. From its first hour, this message crossed every boundary people build.

familyQuestion: The first command of the final revelation was Iqra — Read. What is your relationship with reading — and could one good book change your family's next year?

title: Three Years of Whispers
subtitle: The secret call — the first believers
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1, pp. 240 and 262 — the private preaching, the first believers
Qur'an 26:214 — 'warn, [O Muhammad], your closest kindred'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4770 — the call from Safa and Abu Lahab

chapters.heading: The Call and the Feast
chapters.body: Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet ﷺ kept his mission hidden for three years, 'according to what reached me', until Allah ordered him to make it public. Ibn Hisham gives Khadijah, who is described as the first to believe in Allah and His Messenger, and then Ali, Zayd ibn Haritha and Abu Bakr their own sections, in that order (the order of the early converts is discussed in the sources). When the command came — 'warn, [O Muhammad], your closest kindred' (26:214) — Muhammad ﷺ climbed Safa and called out to the clans of Quraysh until they gathered, and asked them: if I told you that horsemen in the valley were about to attack you, would you believe me? They said: yes, we have never known you to say anything but the truth. He said: then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment. Abu Lahab cursed him and asked whether he had gathered them for this, and Surah al-Masad (111:1-5) was revealed (Bukhari 4770). Accounts of a meal for Banu Hashim in which Ali is said to have answered the call are contested in the sources and were not checked here, so they are not told.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The first believers were a woman, a teenager, and a freed slave. What does that tell you about whose hearts Allah chooses first?

title: Bilal and the Heavy Sand
subtitle: The slave who taught the world a word: Ahad
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 317-318 (the torture of the oppressed; Bilal; Abu Bakr frees six), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: Ahad, Ahad
chapters.body: When the call went public and Quraysh could not bribe or debate it down, they turned on believers who had no clan to shield them. Ibn Ishaq says they tortured the oppressed with beating, hunger, thirst and the heat of Makkah's sand (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 317). Bilal's master was Umayyah ibn Khalaf; at midday Bilal was laid on his back in the valley of Makkah with a great rock on his chest and told he would stay so until he died or denied Muhammad ﷺ, and he kept saying: Ahad, Ahad — One, One (p. 318). Abu Bakr told Umayyah to fear Allah, and offered him a stronger black slave of his own in exchange; Umayyah accepted and Abu Bakr freed Bilal. Ibn Hisham lists six whom Abu Bakr freed at that time, among them Amir ibn Fuhayra, Umm Ubays and Zunayra (p. 318). Bilal, Ammar, Sumayyah, Suhayb, Khabbab: the weak of Makkah are remembered because the truth did not need the strong to survive. It needed the sincere.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Bilal had one word under a boulder: Ahad. If your faith cost you comfort today, what would your one word be?

title: The Night of the Journey
subtitle: Al-Isra wal-Mi'raj — five prayers as the gift of the heavens
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 349 — the full narration of the Night Journey
Qur'an 17:1 — 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night'
Sahih Muslim 162 — the fifty prayers reduced to five

chapters.heading: From the Haram to the Farthest Mosque
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ was carried from the sacred mosque to the farthest mosque in a single night: 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed' (17:1). From Jerusalem he ascended through the heavens — Bukhari preserves the narration in full — past Adam at the first heaven, Isa and Yahya, Yusuf, Idris, Harun, Musa, and Ibrahim leaning against the Bayt al-Ma'mur, to the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary. Musa asked him at the end what his nation had been given, and when he heard fifty prayers a day, Musa said: your people cannot bear fifty — go back and ask your Lord to lighten it (Bukhari 349, Muslim 162). He returned and returned again, until the covenant stood at five prayers for the reward of fifty — until, in the narration, the word came: they are five, and they are fifty; My word is not changed (Muslim 162). The five daily prayers are not a burden negotiated down. They are a gift negotiated up — from the Lord of the heavens, through the stubborn love of Musa for the believers, to your doorstep five times a day.

familyQuestion: Five prayers were gifted from above the seven heavens. Do you treat them as a burden negotiated down — or a gift you get to keep?

title: The Boycott
subtitle: Three years in the valley — the written siege
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1, pp. 350-352 and 374-377 — the document of the boycott and its undoing

chapters.heading: A Document Against a Clan
chapters.body: When persuasion and pressure had not worked, Quraysh tried isolation. Ibn Ishaq records that they gathered and agreed a covenant against Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib: no one would marry into them or give them women in marriage, and no one would sell to them or buy from them. They wrote it in a document and hung it inside the Kaaba to make it binding (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, p. 350). Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib gathered around Abu Talib in his shi'b, the ravine where they were shut in (vol. 1, p. 351). Hisham ibn Amr, whose mother's side was linked to Banu Hashim, would bring a camel loaded with food to the ravine at night and send it in. Then he went to Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayya, al-Mut'im ibn Adi, Abu al-Bakhtari and Zam'a ibn al-Aswad, one by one, until they agreed to meet by night above Makkah to undo the document. Zuhayr circled the Kaaba seven times and vowed not to sit down until the cruel document was torn; Abu Jahl called him a liar. When al-Mut'im went to tear it, he found that termites had eaten it except for the words 'bismika Allahumma' (in Your name, O God) (vol. 1, pp. 375-376). Another report in the same book has Abu Talib tell Quraysh that the Prophet ﷺ had said Allah had sent termites against their document, and the document was torn and its terms cancelled. An editor's note adds that the believers in the ravine suffered severe hunger, eating leaves and scraps. How long the confinement lasted is not stated in the pages read here.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The boycott starved the Muslims for three years but broke before their faith did. What pressure are you under that only feels permanent?

title: The First Hijrah
subtitle: Abyssinia — the king whose bishops wept and refused the extradition
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1, pp. 321 and 333-337 — the emigration to Abyssinia, the envoys, Ja'far before the Negus

chapters.heading: A Kingdom That Let Them Pray
chapters.body: When the suffering of his companions was more than he could shield them from, the Prophet ﷺ told them, as Ibn Ishaq reports: go to the land of Abyssinia, for there is a king there under whom no one is wronged — a land of truth — until Allah grants you relief (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, p. 321). It was the first emigration of the Muslim community: no army, no land promised, just a just king. When the emigrants had found safety there, Quraysh sent Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'a and Amr ibn al-As with Makkan leather and other gifts for the Negus and for each of his bishops, with instructions to give each bishop his gift before speaking and to ask for the Muslims to be handed over before they were heard (vol. 1, pp. 333-335, from Umm Salama's account). The Negus took an oath and refused to surrender them without hearing them. He summoned the Muslims and his bishops, who spread their scriptures around him, and asked what religion they had left their people for. Ja'far ibn Abi Talib answered, describing what they had been and what the Messenger ﷺ had called them to, and when the Negus asked if they had anything from Allah, he recited the opening of Surah Maryam. The Negus wept until his beard was wet, the bishops wept until their scriptures were wet, and he said that this and what Isa brought came from one niche. He told the two envoys to go and would not surrender the Muslims to them (vol. 1, pp. 335-337). The next day Amr tried again with a question about Isa; Ja'far answered that he is Allah's servant, His messenger, His spirit and His word, and the Negus struck the ground with a stick and said Isa did not exceed what Ja'far had said by the width of that stick, and that the Muslims were safe in his land. A Christian kingdom had become the first refuge of Islam.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Negus protected strangers he had no reason to protect. Have you ever been protected by a stranger — or been one for someone else?

title: The Conversion of Umar
subtitle: The man who set out to kill the Prophet ﷺ became his shield
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 343-345 (the conversion narrative up to the knock at the door), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 3680 — the Prophet's ﷺ dream of Umar's palace in Paradise

chapters.heading: A Lion Changes Direction
chapters.body: Umar ibn al-Khattab set out, girded with his sword, to kill the Prophet ﷺ (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 343). On the way Nu'aym ibn Abdullah, who was secretly Muslim, sent him to his own house first: Khabbab used to visit his sister Fatima bint al-Khattab to teach her the Qur'an, and her husband Sa'id ibn Zayd was also a Muslim (pp. 343-344). Umar struck his sister and wounded her; a page headed 'Ta-Ha' was in the house (p. 344). Then, in this account, he washed because she said only the pure may touch it, took the page and read it, and said: how fine this speech is, and how noble (p. 345). Khabbab came out and told him of the Prophet's ﷺ prayer that Islam be strengthened by Abu al-Hakam ibn Hisham or by Umar ibn al-Khattab, and said the Prophet was in a house by Safa. Umar took his sword and went to that house and knocked at the door (p. 345). The account runs on to the moment he accepts Islam on the next page, which was not read for this audit. The Prophet's ﷺ dream of a palace in Paradise that he was told was Umar's is in Sahih al-Bukhari 3680.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Umar went to the door with a sword and was met by a page of the Qur'an. When did something you read change the errand you were on?

title: Taif
subtitle: Driven to a vineyard — and he hoped for their descendants
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 419-420 (the journey to Ta'if; the vineyard; the supplication), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 — the day of Aqabah and the angel of the mountains

chapters.heading: The Saddest Day of the Seerah
chapters.body: After Abu Talib died, Quraysh harmed the Prophet ﷺ more than they had before, and he went out to Ta'if to seek the support of Thaqif (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 419). Thaqif stirred up their fools and slaves against him, cursing and shouting at him, and drove him into a vineyard belonging to Utba and Shayba, sons of Rabi'a (p. 420). There, in Ibn Ishaq's account, he prayed: 'O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness, my lack of resources and my humiliation before the people... If You are not displeased with me, then I do not care' (p. 420). In another report Aisha asks whether he had faced a day harder than Uhud, and he answers that the worst was the day of Aqabah; the angel of the mountains is offered to him at Qarn al-Tha'alib, and he declines, hoping that Allah will bring from their descendants people who worship Allah alone (Bukhari 3231; the hadith itself does not name Ta'if or mention stones). Other reports, not checked here: that he was stoned and bled, that the mountain-angel scene took place on this journey, and that a delegation from Ta'if later accepted Islam.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The man they stoned prayed for their grandchildren. Is there someone who hurt you whose children you could still bless?

title: The Pledges of Aqabah
subtitle: Seventy-five hands in the dark — Madinah accepts the message
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 429, 433, 434, 441 and 443 (the six, the twelve, Mus'ab, the second pledge, the twelve leaders), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 18 — the pledge of Aqabah: no shirk, theft, adultery, killing children, slander or disobedience in good (narrated by Ubadah ibn al-Samit)

chapters.heading: Twelve, Then Seventy-Five
chapters.body: At the pilgrimage season the Prophet ﷺ met six men of the Khazraj at Aqabah, among them As'ad ibn Zurara and Rafi' ibn Malik. Ibn Ishaq says they told one another that this was the prophet the Jews had threatened them with, and that they had left a people among whom there was enmity and evil, hoping Allah would unite them through him (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 429). The next year twelve men met him at Aqabah. Ubada ibn al-Samit says: 'we were twelve men', and the pledge was the like of the women's pledge, before fighting was prescribed: not to associate anything with Allah, not to steal, not to commit adultery, not to kill their children (p. 433; also Sahih al-Bukhari 18, in the wording: no shirk, theft, adultery, killing children, slander or disobedience in good). The Prophet ﷺ sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr with them, ordering him to teach them the Qur'an and Islam and to give them understanding in the religion; Asim ibn Umar reports that he used to lead them in prayer (p. 434). The next year the pilgrims of Yathrib came again; a narrator says: 'we were seventy-three men, and with us two women', and that they slipped out secretly after a third of the night and gathered in the ravine at Aqabah, where al-Abbas, still on his people's religion, spoke first and asked them to protect his nephew only if they could keep their promise (p. 441). The Prophet ﷺ then had twelve leaders chosen, nine from the Khazraj and three from the Aws (p. 443). The Ansar of Madinah were preparing a city before the Prophet ﷺ had ever seen it.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Ansar believed in a man they had met twice. What makes someone trustworthy enough to follow?

title: The Hijrah
subtitle: The cave, the companion, and the man who rode for a bounty
sources: Qur'an 9:40 — 'as one of two, when they were in the cave' (revealed for this night)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 — the Hijrah with Abu Bakr, including three nights in the cave
Sahih al-Bukhari 3653 — Abu Bakr in the cave: 'what do you think of two whose third is Allah'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3906 — Suraqa, the sinking horse and the written pledge
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa, al-Abyari and al-Shalabi), vol. 1 pp. 482, 485, 489-490 and 492, read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The Second of Two
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ left Makkah with Abu Bakr and entered a cave in Mount Thawr, below the city (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 485). Ibn Ishaq, as Ibn Hisham gives it, has Abu Jahl propose that Quraysh take one strong, well-born young man from every clan to strike together, so that Banu Abd Manaf could not fight all of Quraysh and would settle for the blood-price (vol. 1 p. 482). In the cave Abu Bakr's son listened by day to what people said of them, and Asma bint Abi Bakr brought food at nightfall (p. 485). Bukhari 3905 has them stay in the cave three nights. In Bukhari 3653 Abu Bakr says that if one of the pursuers looked down at his own feet he would see them, and the Prophet ﷺ answers: what do you think of two whose third is Allah? The Qur'an keeps his words: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us', and says Allah supported him with soldiers you did not see (9:40). Later tradition adds a spider's web and a dove's nest at the entrance; these are not in the Qur'an, in Bukhari 3905 or in the pages read, and no chain was verified for this audit. Ibn Hisham reports Quraysh offering a hundred camels to whoever brought him back (p. 489). In Suraqa ibn Malik's own account there, his horse stumbled and threw him three times, and the third time its forelegs sank into the ground; he asked for a written pledge, and the Prophet ﷺ told Abu Bakr to write it, on a bone, a scrap or a potsherd (pp. 489-490). Suraqa put it in his quiver, went back and kept silent about what he had seen. Bukhari 3906 also has the horse's forelegs sink and the written pledge. The two reached Quba, among Banu Amr ibn Awf, on a Monday in Rabi' al-Awwal; Ibn Hisham gives the twelfth night, and a footnote notes that some say the eighth (p. 492).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Allah's help in the cave came without any visible guard. What unseen help have you only noticed looking back?

title: The Arrival in Madinah
subtitle: The city rejoiced: the Messenger has arrived
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 494-496 (Quba, the camel, Abu Ayyub), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 3925 — the joy of Madinah at his arrival (al-Bara' ibn Azib)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2048 — Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: half the wealth, 'show me the market'
Qur'an 9:108 — 'a mosque founded on righteousness from the first day'

chapters.heading: A City That Ran to Meet Him
chapters.body: At Quba the Prophet ﷺ stayed, by Ibn Hisham's account, from Monday to Thursday (Banu Amr ibn Awf claimed he stayed longer) and founded his mosque there, which a footnote calls the first mosque built in Islam (vol. 1 p. 494); the Qur'an honors a mosque 'founded on righteousness from the first day' (9:108). Then he rode toward Madinah. Clan after clan stopped his camel and invited him to stay with them, speaking of their numbers, strength and protection, and each time he answered: 'Let her go her way, for she is commanded' (pp. 494-495). The camel knelt at the gate of the mosque-site in the house of Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar; he did not dismount, it rose, walked a little, then turned back and knelt in the same place, and he got down; Abu Ayyub al-Ansari carried his saddle into his house (pp. 495-496). Al-Bara' ibn Azib said he had never seen the people of Madinah rejoice as they did: even the slave girls were saying that the Messenger of Allah had arrived (Bukhari 3925). The Ansar and Muhajirun were paired as brothers. In one hadith the Ansari Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' offered Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf half of his wealth; Abd al-Rahman declined and asked only where the market was, and the Prophet ﷺ later told him to hold a wedding feast, even with one sheep (Bukhari 2048). The first economy of Madinah, then, began with an offer of half and an answer of 'show me the market'.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Sa'd offered half of everything and Abd al-Rahman asked only for the market. What would you genuinely share, and what would you refuse and still be grateful for?

title: The Charter of Madinah
subtitle: One document, one ummah — many faiths under one covenant
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1, pp. 501-503 — the text of the document between the Muhajirun, the Ansar and the Jews
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, p. 516 — the Islam of Abdullah ibn Salam
Qur'an 63:1 — the hypocrites

chapters.heading: Writing a Nation
chapters.body: After the Hijra, the Prophet ﷺ did something no conqueror does: Ibn Ishaq gives the text of a document he wrote between the Muhajirun and the Ansar and made a truce with the Jews of Madinah, confirming them in their religion and property (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, pp. 501-503). It opens in the name of Allah, binds the believers and Muslims of Quraysh and Yathrib and those who follow and fight alongside them, and declares them one community apart from other people. The Jews of Banu Awf are one community with the believers: the Jews have their religion and the Muslims theirs; Jews and believers each bear their own expenses and spend alongside one another while they fight together; they support one another against whoever attacks the people of the document; Yathrib is sacred to them; and any dispute is to be referred to Allah and to Muhammad. The same status is given to a list of other Jewish clans. Abdullah ibn Salam, a learned Jewish rabbi of Madinah, embraced Islam when the Prophet ﷺ arrived (Ibn Ishaq's account, from members of his family, vol. 1, p. 516). The Qur'an speaks of the hypocrites of Madinah, those who said with their mouths what their hearts denied (63:1). Ibn Hisham also lists Jewish leaders of several clans who were hostile to the Prophet ﷺ, except Abdullah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq (vol. 1, p. 516). How the covenant fared afterwards is not told here because it was not checked. But the document itself stands in the reports that preserve it: an early written covenant for a plural city.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Charter made one nation of different faiths. What community are you part of that needs one covenant more than it needs one religion?

title: The Qibla Changes
subtitle: Sixteen months toward Jerusalem — then one command turned a congregation around
sources: Qur'an 2:142-150 — the whole passage, 'We see the turning of your face'
Sahih al-Bukhari 399 — the change of the qiblah

chapters.heading: Turning the Whole Community
chapters.body: For sixteen or seventeen months in Madinah (Bukhari 399), the Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem — the qiblah of Ibrahim and Musa. Some people were not content with it. And the Prophet ﷺ, who used to face the heavens waiting for the command, received it mid-prayer: a prayer (placing it in a zuhr prayer at the mosque of Banu Salama is a later tradition we have not verified), during which the verse descended — 'So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram' (2:144) — and the worshippers turned toward Makkah mid-prayer (Bukhari 399). Allah framed the change itself as revelation about revelation: 'We have certainly seen the turning of your face, [O Muhammad], toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased' (2:144) — and then taught the deeper lesson: it is not righteousness to face east or west (2:177). And the fools said, 'What has turned them from their qiblah?' — to which the answer came: 'Say, To Allah belongs the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path' (2:142).

familyQuestion: The whole congregation turned mid-prayer without arguing. When has your community changed direction without splitting?

title: Badr: The Two Armies Meet
subtitle: A little over three hundred against some nine hundred to a thousand
sources: Qur'an 3:123-127 — 'already had Allah given you victory at'
Qur'an 8:41 — 'that which We sent down to Our Servant on the day of criterion'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3959 — the companions at Badr numbered over three hundred and ten (al-Bara')
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 617, 626 and 627, read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The Criterion
chapters.body: The Qur'an later named the day: 'the day of criterion - the day when the two armies met' (8:41). The Muslims were a little over three hundred and ten (Bukhari 3959, from al-Bara'), against Quraysh, whom a scout reported as between nine hundred and a thousand (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 617). On the morning of the battle the Prophet ﷺ was straightening the ranks with an arrow in his hand; he prodded Sawad ibn Ghaziyya in the belly to bring him into line, and Sawad asked to take his retaliation, which the Prophet ﷺ allowed (p. 626). Then, in the shelter built for him, he pleaded with his Lord for the victory promised: 'O Allah, if this band perishes today You will not be worshipped'; Abu Bakr told him that was enough pleading, for Allah would fulfil what He promised (p. 627). The Qur'an records the other side of that morning: 'already had Allah given you victory at' Badr 'while you were few in number' (3:123). Three thousand angels, it says — 'to reassure your hearts thereby. And victory is not except from Allah' (3:126).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Allah sent angels but said victory is only from Him. When you win, who do you thank first?

title: Badr: The Prisoners
subtitle: The prisoners of Badr: 'treat them well'
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 p. 645 (the prisoners distributed; 'treat them well'; Abu Aziz and the bread), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Qur'an 8:67-71 — 'It is not for a prophet to have captives'

chapters.heading: Mercy After Victory
chapters.body: The battle was over and the prisoners were taken. Ibn Ishaq reports that the Prophet ﷺ distributed the prisoners among his companions and said: 'Treat the prisoners well' (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 645). Abu Aziz ibn Umayr, one of them, later said that the men who held him gave him the bread at their meals while they ate dates themselves (p. 645). A report that the Prophet ﷺ set the ransom of some literate prisoners at teaching Muslim children to read is told elsewhere; it is not on the pages read here and its source was not checked. The revelation that came about the day named the tension honestly: 'It is not for a prophet to have captives' (8:67). But the surah goes on to the law that outlasted the battle: 'So consume what you have taken of war booty' (8:69), and calls it 'lawful and good' — and to the prisoners themselves: 'and He will forgive you' (8:70), if Allah knows good in their hearts.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ told his companions to treat their prisoners well, and they gave them the bread. When did you last do the generous thing for someone who had lost to you?

title: Uhud: The Day the Line Broke
subtitle: Archers leave the pass — and the Prophet ﷺ bleeds on the mountain
sources: Qur'an 3:152-155 — the day 'some of you desired the world'
Qur'an 3:144 — 'Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4043-4044 — the archers who left their post at Uhud

chapters.heading: The Turning
chapters.body: The archers held the pass behind the Muslims as ordered — until the spoils of the routed enemy appeared, and most of them descended, against orders, for their share. Khalid ibn al-Walid, still an enemy commander that day, saw the pass empty and wheeled his cavalry through it. The Muslim line broke from behind; Hamza, the master of martyrs, fell; and the Prophet ﷺ — wounded in the face, a tooth broken, rumor running the field that he had been killed — stood on the slope with the remnant around him. The verse descended that anchors the whole religion: 'Muhammad is not but a messenger. [Other] messengers have passed on before him. So if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels [to unbelief]?' (3:144). The Muslims rallied to the slope; the Quraysh withdrew. And the revelation's verdict on the day named the lesson every generation inherits: 'And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing the enemy by His permission until [the time] when you lost courage and fell to disputing about the order [given by the Prophet] and disobeyed after He had shown you that which you love' (3:152) — victory had come by obedience; its near-loss came by desire. The spoils of Uhud were a Qur'an.

familyQuestion: The archers left their post for spoils and nearly lost everything. What 'post' are you tempted to leave right now?

title: Uhud: Hamza and the Women
subtitle: The master of martyrs, the mutilated dead, and Hind's answer
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 91, 95-96 (Hind; the Prophet and Hamza; the prohibition of mutilation), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 4072 — Wahshi's account of killing Hamza
Sahih al-Bukhari 3825 — Hind bint Utba after she embraced Islam
Qur'an 16:126-128 — 'punish with an equivalent of that with which you were harmed'

chapters.heading: The Lion and the Lesson
chapters.body: Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle, was killed at Uhud by a thrown spear: Wahshi, a slave of Jubayr ibn Mut'im who had been promised his freedom for it, tells how he drove the spear in (Bukhari 4072). Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet ﷺ went looking for him and found him in the valley with his belly cut open, his liver taken out, his nose and ears cut off (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 95). Ibn Hisham also names Hind bint Utba as the one who made anklets and necklaces from the ears and noses of the dead and who cut into Hamza's liver (p. 91). Ibn Ishaq has the Prophet ﷺ say, seeing him, that were it not for Safiyya's grief and for the precedent it would set, he would leave him for the beasts and the birds (p. 95); and then swear that if Allah gave him victory over Quraysh he would mutilate thirty of their men (pp. 95-96). The Muslims said the same. Then came the revelation: 'punish with an equivalent of that with which you were harmed. But if you are patient - it is better for those who are patient' (16:126). Ibn Hisham states that the Prophet ﷺ forbade mutilation (p. 96). Hind bint Utba later came to him and said that before she embraced Islam there was no household on earth she wished to see disgraced more than his, and now none she wished to see honored more (Bukhari 3825).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ was told that patience is better than the revenge he had sworn. What revenge habit could your family end with you?

title: The Trench
subtitle: Ten thousand at the walls — and a biting wind from the unseen
sources: Qur'an 33:9-27 — '[Remember] when they came at you from above you and from below you'
Qur'an 33:10-11 — 'there the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking'
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 2, pp. 215-233 — the Battle of the Trench

chapters.heading: The Severe Shaking
chapters.body: In Shawwal of the fifth year, according to Ibn Ishaq (the date is disputed), men of Banu al-Nadir and Banu Wa'il went to Makkah and urged Quraysh to fight the Prophet ﷺ, and then to Ghatafan; Quraysh marched under Abu Sufyan, and Ghatafan under chiefs including Uyayna ibn Hisn and al-Harith ibn Awf (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, pp. 215-216). The Prophet ﷺ ordered a trench dug around Madinah and worked on the digging himself; some hypocrites hung back and slipped away to their families without leave. It is said that Salman the Persian suggested the trench, and when the Quraysh horsemen saw it they called it a stratagem the Arabs had not used (vol. 2, p. 224). The allies camped at Majma' al-Asyal, ten thousand by Ibn Hisham's count (vol. 2, p. 219). As the siege tightened and fear spread, a man named Mu'attib ibn Qushayr said: Muhammad used to promise us the treasures of Kisra and Caesar, and today none of us feels safe going out to relieve himself (vol. 2, p. 222). There was little fighting beyond arrows and a blockade, though a few Quraysh horsemen forced their horses across a narrow part of the trench and Ali killed Amr ibn Abd Wudd (vol. 2, pp. 223-225). The Qur'an preserved the city at its breaking point: '[Remember] when they came at you from above you and from below you, and when eyes shifted [in fear], and hearts reached the throats and you assumed about Allah [various] assumptions. There the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking' (33:10-11). Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud came to the Prophet ﷺ and said he had become Muslim but his people did not know; the Prophet ﷺ told him to sow discord among the enemy if he could, and he went to Banu Qurayza (vol. 2, p. 229). Then Allah sowed discord among the allies, and sent a very cold wind on a winter night that overturned their pots and threw down their tents; Abu Sufyan called on Quraysh to leave, and Ghatafan turned back for their own land (vol. 2, pp. 231-233; the Qur'an mentions the wind and the soldiers in 33:9). The Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims returned to Madinah. Madinah had not won the Trench by arms alone: the Qur'an credits Allah with sending the wind (33:9).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The trench held because Salman, a Persian outsider, was listened to. Whose 'outsider' idea are you ignoring right now?

title: Hudaybiyyah
subtitle: The treaty that looked like defeat — and the sura named a clear conquest
sources: Qur'an 48:1-3 — 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest'
Sahih al-Bukhari 2731-2732 — the terms of the treaty of Hudaybiyyah and Umar's objection
Sahih al-Bukhari 4154 — about fourteen hundred men (Jabir)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4177 — a sura revealed on the journey (Al-Fath)
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 316-318 (the truce, the ten years, Umar's question and the reply), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The Clear Conquest
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ set out for Makkah to perform umrah in peace with about fourteen hundred men (Bukhari 4154, from Jabir) — and Quraysh barred them from the House at Hudaybiyyah (Bukhari 2731). The treaty that followed looked like surrender. Quraysh insisted that he go back that year (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 316). In the text Ibn Hisham gives, the two sides agreed to put war away from the people for ten years, in which people would be safe; and a man of Quraysh who came to Muhammad without his guardian's permission would be returned, while one who went to Quraysh would not (p. 317). Bukhari 2731 has the same clause that Suhayl demanded, even if the man had embraced Islam. Umar ibn al-Khattab could not bear it. In Bukhari 2731 he asks whether their cause is not the right one and the enemy's wrong. In Ibn Hisham he asks: why should we accept humiliation in our religion? And the Prophet ﷺ answers: 'I am the servant of Allah and His Messenger; I will not disobey His command, and He will not let me be lost' (p. 317). Bukhari 4177 records that on a night journey a sura was revealed to him and he recited its opening: the sura of Al-Fath, which Bukhari files under the Hudaybiyyah expedition. The Qur'an named what no eye could see: 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest' (48:1). Two years later the Muslims entered Makkah.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The treaty everyone hated opened the doors of Arabia. Have you ever had a 'defeat' that was actually a door?

title: The Letters to the Rulers
subtitle: The letter that reached the Emperor of Rome
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 2, p. 607 — the envoys and the kings they were sent to
Sahih al-Bukhari 2941 — the letter to Heraclius and Abu Sufyan's questioning
Sahih al-Bukhari 64 — Kisra tears the letter

chapters.heading: From the Prophet of Mercy
chapters.body: During the truce with Quraysh, the Prophet ﷺ began writing to the rulers around him. Ibn Hisham lists the envoys and the kings: Dihya al-Kalbi to Caesar, king of the Romans; Abdullah ibn Hudhafa al-Sahmi to Kisra, king of Persia; Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri to the Negus of Abyssinia; Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a to al-Muqawqis of Alexandria; and others to the rulers of Oman, al-Yamama, Bahrain and the Syrian frontier (vol. 2, p. 607). The letter to Heraclius is preserved in the Sahih: it greets those who follow guidance, calls him to Islam, promises that if he accepts he will be safe and Allah will give him his reward twice, and warns that if he turns away the sin of his people (the tillers, as the translation glosses it) is on him, and it ends by calling the People of the Scripture to worship Allah alone (Bukhari 2941). The same hadith, from Abu Sufyan, tells how Heraclius, at Ilya (Jerusalem), had Abu Sufyan, who was in Syria on trade during the truce, summoned and questioned him through an interpreter about the Prophet's ﷺ lineage, his followers, whether he had been known to lie, and his teachings (Bukhari 2941). Kisra took the Prophet's letter, read it and tore it, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed against them (Bukhari 64). What each of the other rulers did with their letters is not told here because it was not checked.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ wrote 'become Muslim and you will be safe' to the most powerful men alive. What does that tell you about the mission — fear, or invitation?

title: The Conquest of Makkah
subtitle: Eight years after being driven out — he enters with his head bowed
sources: Qur'an 110 — 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4280 — Abu Sufyan sees the Muslim forces enter Makkah; the Prophet's ﷺ flag at al-Hajun
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 400, 406, 409, 412 and 413 (the march, the entry, the orders, the address, the pictures), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The Day of Mercy
chapters.body: In Ramadan of the eighth year the Prophet ﷺ camped at Marr al-Zahran with ten thousand Muslims (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 400). Bukhari 4280 has Abu Sufyan watching the Muslim forces pass. He ordered his commanders to fight only those who fought them, and named a few individuals who were to be killed (p. 409). The army went in by separate roads; when Sa'd ibn Ubada said that today was a day of slaughter, Umar warned the Prophet ﷺ, who stood to answer (p. 406). Ibn Hisham gives the Prophet's ﷺ address to Quraysh: he asked what they thought he would do with them, they answered with kindness, and he said: 'Go, for you are the freed ones' (p. 412). He ordered the pictures in the House effaced (p. 413). Surah An-Nasr speaks of that victory: 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes' and then to 'ask forgiveness of Him. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance' (110:1-3). Other details told of the day, not checked here: his head lowered on his mount, reciting Al-Fath; the idols of the Kaaba cast down by his hand; the Qurayshi breach of the truce that began the campaign.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: He entered the city that tried to kill him and said 'you are free.' Who in your life deserves amnesty you have the power to give?

title: Hunayn and Taif
subtitle: Victory at Hunayn, and a city that later came to Islam
sources: Qur'an 9:25-27 — 'Allah has already given you victory in many regions'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4333 — Hunayn, the spoils and the Prophet's ﷺ words to the Ansar
Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 — 'I hope that Allah will let them beget children who will worship Allah alone'
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 2, pp. 437-438, 478, 484, 537 — Hawazin at Hunayn, Ta'if, the delegation of Thaqif

chapters.heading: The Spoils and the Sweetness
chapters.body: After Makkah came Hunayn, against Hawazin and their allies under Malik ibn Awf, who had brought their property, women and children with them to Awtas (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, pp. 437-438). The Qur'an speaks of the day when the Muslims' numbers pleased them yet availed them nothing, and of Allah sending down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and the believers (9:25-27); in the hadith the Muslims first retreated and the Prophet ﷺ called the Ansar, who pledged themselves to him, and the Muslims defeated the pagans (Bukhari 4333). He gave the spoils to the Tulaqa' (the recently converted Makkans) and the Muhajirun, and nothing to the Ansar, who were dissatisfied. He gathered them in a leather tent and said: are you not pleased that the people return with sheep and camels while you return with the Messenger of Allah? And if the people walked one path and the Ansar another, he would take the Ansar's path (Bukhari 4333; the Ansar's reply is not recorded in that report). Then the Prophet ﷺ marched to Ta'if, where the defeated Thaqif had shut their gates (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, p. 478). During the siege he told Abu Bakr his dream of a bowl of butter that a rooster pecked and spilled; he told Umar he had not been given permission against Thaqif, and the army departed without taking the city (vol. 2, p. 484). In Ramadan of the ninth year, after Tabuk, a delegation of Thaqif came to him and they accepted Islam (vol. 2, p. 537). The hope he voiced on the day Ibn Abd Yalil turned him away — that Allah would let them beget children who would worship Allah alone — is recorded in Bukhari 3231.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Ansar were offered 'the Messenger of Allah' instead of wealth — and wept with joy. What would you take in place of money?

title: Tabuk
subtitle: The hardest march — and the hypocrites unmasked
sources: Qur'an 9:38-59 — the whole passage of the expedition
Qur'an 9:117-118 — 'Then He turned to them so they could repent'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4418 — Ka'b ibn Malik's account of Tabuk and the three who stayed behind
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 2, pp. 515-517 — the order to prepare for Tabuk and those who held back

chapters.heading: The Expedition of Hardship
chapters.body: In the heat of the ripening fruit season, with the shade pleasant and the journey long, the Prophet ﷺ ordered the Muslims to prepare to fight the Romans — Tabuk, in the year nine. He rarely named his destination ahead of time; this time he made it clear, because of the distance, the hardship and the size of the enemy (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, p. 516; Bukhari 4418). Al-Jadd ibn Qays asked to be excused, saying, in the verse's words, 'Permit me [to remain at home] and do not put me to trial' (9:49), and some hypocrites told one another not to march in the heat, which the Qur'an answers in 9:81-82 (vol. 2, pp. 516-517). The Qur'an unmasked such excuses in Surah At-Tawbah: 'If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and will replace you with another people' (9:39). In Ka'b ibn Malik's own account, around eighty men gave excuses and oaths, which the Prophet ﷺ accepted; Ka'b and two others, Murara ibn al-Rabi' and Hilal ibn Umayya, were left pending. The Prophet ﷺ ordered the Muslims not to speak to the three, and it lasted fifty nights, until at dawn on the fiftieth morning a voice announced that their repentance had been accepted (Bukhari 4418; the Qur'an: 9:118, 'the three who were left behind ... Then He turned to them so they could repent'). Ka'b adds that the verse refers to the deferral of their case. The lesson stands near the summit of the seerah: the community is measured not by the battles it wins but by the accountability it survives — even believers who stayed behind without a valid excuse were disciplined publicly, and their repentance was written into the Qur'an.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Ka'b ibn Malik's punishment became a verse of forgiveness. What mistake of yours could become your testimony?

title: The Farewell Sermon
subtitle: One speech, one standing — the charter of every Muslim generation
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 67 — the Prophet's ﷺ sermon on the sanctity of lives, wealth and honor
Sahih Muslim 1218 — Jabir's account of the Prophet's ﷺ Hajj and the Farewell address

chapters.heading: Listen Well, for I May Not Meet You Again Here
chapters.body: In the tenth year, the Prophet ﷺ performed his only full pilgrimage, and at Arafat, standing on his camel, he delivered the sermon that is the constitution of the ummah. The tradition preserves it: every Muslim's blood, property, and honor are inviolable, like this day, in this month, in this city; no usury from this day; no blood feud from this day; women have rights over you as you have rights over them; your brother's blood and property are sacred (Bukhari 67, Muslim 1218). Then he asked: have I conveyed? — and the valley answered: yes. And he raised his finger to the sky and said: O Allah, bear witness; O Allah, bear witness. And he told them, while he still stood before them healthy: those who are present must convey it to those who are absent — and he would be with them for only a few months more. The sermon of Arafat is remembered because it gathers, in one address, the dignity of life, wealth and honor.

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ said your brother's blood and property are sacred. Whose rights are you trampling right now without noticing?

title: The Passing of the Prophet ﷺ
subtitle: The house of Aisha, the sword of Umar, and the steadiness of Abu Bakr
sources: Qur'an 3:144 — 'if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels [to unbelief]'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4437 — Aisha: 'with the highest companion'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3668 — Umar's denial and Abu Bakr's words and recitation
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 2, pp. 642-655 — the illness and the day of his death

chapters.heading: Monday
chapters.body: After the farewell pilgrimage and the sending of Usama's army, the illness began, in the last nights of Safar or the start of Rabi' al-Awwal according to Ibn Ishaq, after a night visit to the cemetery of al-Baqi'; he asked his wives' leave to be nursed in the house of Aisha (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, pp. 642-643, 649). When he fell ill he ordered that Abu Bakr lead the people in prayer (vol. 2, p. 652). On Monday, the day God took him, he lifted the curtain and stood at the door of Aisha's room while the people prayed Subh, and smiled at them; in another report on the same page Abu Bakr was leading and stepped back, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed seated beside him (vol. 2, p. 653). He asked, as Aisha reports, to be with the Highest Companion (Bukhari 4437, with his head on her thigh; Ibn Hisham has him dying with his head against her chest and throat, vol. 2, p. 655). Umar stood and refused to believe it: he has not died; he has gone to his Lord as Musa went (vol. 2, p. 655; Bukhari 3668). Abu Bakr came from al-Sunh, uncovered the Prophet's ﷺ face, kissed him and praised him in life and death, and told the people: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worshipped Allah, Allah is living and never dies — then he recited 'Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him' (3:144) (Bukhari 3668). The Ansar gathered at the shed of Banu Sa'ida to discuss leadership, and Umar pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr and the people followed (Bukhari 3668). The Prophet ﷺ died in the house of Aisha, on her day. The tradition records that the day was Monday — the day of his birth.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Umar denied it; Abu Bakr recited Qur'an. When grief hits your family, which one will you be?

title: What He Left
subtitle: No palace, no hoard, no empire in his name — and an ummah that outlives empires
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 2739 — the Prophet ﷺ left no money, only his mule, his weapons and a charitable land endowment
Sahih al-Bukhari 3092 — 'what we leave is charity'
Sahih al-Bukhari 2068 — grain bought on credit from a Jew with his armour as a pledge
Sunan Ibn Majah 2697 — the last counsel: the prayer (da'if per Darussalam)

chapters.heading: The Inventory of a Prophet
chapters.body: When he died he left no money, no male or female slave, and nothing but his white mule, his weapons, and a piece of land he had given in charity (Sahih al-Bukhari 2739). He had bought food grain from a Jew on credit and given his iron armour as a pledge (Sahih al-Bukhari 2068). A report preserves his last counsel as: the prayer, and those whom your right hands possess (Ibn Majah 2697, graded da'if by Darussalam). He left no inheritance to divide: 'Our property will not be inherited; whatever we leave is sadaqa' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3092). Abu Bakr cited those words to Fatima when she asked for her share, and he refused any property of the Prophet's ﷺ. The inventory is short on purpose: a mule, weapons, a plot given away, and a message.

familyQuestion: He left no inheritance but character. What will your children inherit from you that money can't buy?

title: Reflections: The Man Who Walked Beside Us
subtitle: Thirty chapters, one walk — what it means to follow him ﷺ
sources: Musnad Ahmad — 'I have only been sent to perfect noble character' (number not verified)
Sahih Muslim 45 — none of you truly believes until he wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself
Qur'an 33:21 — 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and [who] remembers Allah often'

chapters.heading: The Example
chapters.body: The Qur'an does not say the Prophet ﷺ was perfect so you could worship him. It says: 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and [who] remembers Allah often' (33:21) — what the Arabic calls uswa hasana. An example is for following. He was an orphan, so the orphan is honored. He was a merchant, so the scale is straight. He was driven from his city, so the stranger is sheltered. He was stoned, so the wounded are comforted. He conquered, so the conquered are forgiven. He ruled, so rulers are accountable. He died poor, so the poor are honored. Thirty chapters walked past like thirty footsteps — and the invitation of every one of them is the same: walk here. Not in his century, but in his character. One way to answer the question — what did he leave us? — is: nothing you can hold, and everything you can become.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Thirty chapters end here. Which single habit of his ﷺ — honesty, gentleness, patience, courage, mercy — will your family practice together this week?

title: Iqra — The First Word
subtitle: The first word of the final message was not 'believe' or 'obey' — it was 'read'
sources: Qur'an 96:1-5

chapters.heading: A Cave, a Covering, a Voice
chapters.body: Muhammad ﷺ had taken to the cave of Hira, seeking quiet from a city that troubled him. In Ramadan, at forty, the angel came to him, pressed him, and said one word: Iqra — the bundled Saheeh International text begins the verse 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created' (96:1). The man who would be called unlettered received a command built on the written word. Whatever else the world would say about this religion, its first word was an act of the mind.

chapters.heading: The Name of Your Lord
chapters.body: The reply to 'I cannot read' was not a scolding. It was the material itself: 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created - Created man from a clinging substance. Recite, and your Lord is the most Generous - Who taught by the pen - Taught man that which he knew not' (96:1-5). Name first, then knowledge. Every act of learning in this deen begins with whose name is on it.

chapters.heading: What the First Word Decided
chapters.body: Notice what the first revelation did not say. Not 'rule', not 'conquer', not 'gather followers'. Read, in the name of your Lord. The command that launched a civilization made literacy an act of worship and inquiry a form of devotion. The Prophet ﷺ came home trembling, and Khadijah held him and said what the moment required: 'Allah will never disgrace you — you keep kinship, you carry the weak.' The first word chose knowledge; the first home chose comfort. The message has lived in both ever since.

familyQuestion: What are we 'reading' in our home this month — and in whose name do we begin?
